checks.//: ═══ FLEET HEALTH — every pack carries these, so the pack runs on its own. None needs crop tuning. ═══

PEACOCK SPOT (Venturia oleaginea). Minimum leaf-wetness periods for infection, Obanor et al. 2011 (Plant Pathology 60:190): 18, 12, 12, 12 and 24 h at 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 °C — tested in 6-h steps, so each true minimum may be up to 6 h shorter. Viruega et al. 2011 (Plant Disease 95:1139) independently puts the optimum at 15.5 °C with an 11.9 h minimum. UC IPM gives infection across 1.7–26.7 °C (35–80 °F) and "as little as 14 hours" near 24 °C (75 °F), so the 20–24 °C band uses 14 h and 24–26.7 °C uses Obanor's 24 h (the two sources disagree there). The entry carries this curve as bands, each holding the longest requirement in it, and counts a wet period by rate summation (each wet hour adds 1 / hours needed at that temperature; the alert raises at 100 %), so a night drifting across a band edge stays one run. Below 5 °C no infection data were found, so the 1.7–5 °C band uses UC IPM's ~48 h for significant disease. Caveats: the data are free-water hours and RH ≥ 90 % is a proxy; Viruega found dry breaks of up to 78 h after wetting did not reduce disease incidence, so a dry spell of up to 12 h (maxDryHours) pauses the count instead of ending it — this pack's conservative reading of that finding; the dry time itself earns nothing. Sources: Obanor et al. 2011 figures as reproduced in https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8231239/ ; UC IPM, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/olive/peacock-spot/

ANTHRACNOSE (Colletotrichum), the mild, rainy-autumn fruit rot. Moral et al. 2012: infects at 10–25 °C, most severe at 17–20 °C, with severity rising steadily across 0–48 h of wetness — there is no single threshold, and 24 h is this pack's choice. UC IPM has no olive anthracnose page. Source: Phytopathology, https://doi.org/10.1094/phyto-12-11-0343

═══ FREEZE ═══ UC (Vossen, "First Press"): ice forms on the fruit at 0 °C and the interior freezes slightly lower; frozen fruit makes defective oil. Trees are broadly hardy to about −9.4 °C (15 °F). UC gives no fruit-freeze number; −1.7 °C (29 °F) is the commonly cited non-UC figure. Source: https://ucanr.edu/sites/default/files/2010-07/27259.pdf

FRUIT AND WOOD FREEZE. Olive fruit can be damaged below 29 °F (−1.7 °C); small wood is injured below 25 °F (−4 °C); trees can die below 15 °F (−9.4 °C). No UC document gives a numeric fruit figure — the 29 °F value is from The Olive Oil Source (which cites the UC Olive Production Manual); the wood figures are UCCE (Vossen). No source gives a duration, so these are single-reading minima. Freeze damage taints oil, and oil olives are harvested November–January, so the fruit entry runs then. Sources: https://www.oliveoilsource.com/info/frost-prevention ; Vossen, UCCE, "Olive Oil Production", https://ucanr.edu/sites/default/files/2010-12/64463.pdf

FROST TONIGHT. FAO Frost Protection (Snyder, UC Davis): start wind machines at about 0 °C, and in any case before the crop's critical temperature. Raised up to 14 h ahead so the decision is made the evening before. DISABLED: needs the top-level forecast block and a Weatherbit key (see README, Forecast).

SOIL pH — olive: outside 6.5–8.5. pH moves over seasons, not hours, so this is info and needs a day sustained; it stays open until the field is limed or acidified. Source: UC ANR, "Soil Nutrient Management for Olives", https://ucanr.edu/sites/default/files/2025-10/Soil%20Nutrient%20Management%20for%20Olives.pdf
